title: Pascal's night of fire (1654)
hookLine: a mathematician has an experience one night and writes Fire, sewing the note into his coat

lines: A NOTE SEWN INTO A COAT.
cards: After Blaise Pascal dies, a servant going through his clothes feels something stiff in the lining of his coat.
Tucked inside, the story goes, is a folded piece of parchment, and inside that, a scrap of paper, both in Pascal's handwriting.
He had sewn it in, and he is said to have moved it from coat to coat, never mentioning it to anyone. Pascal was a mathematician and inventor, a man of numbers and proofs. But the note isn't a proof.
It's barely sentences. Near the top, one word.

teach.h: FIRE: TWO HOURS IN THE NIGHT.
teach.b: The word is Fire. The note gives the hours: from about half past ten at night until about half past midnight. Pascal didn't try to explain what happened.
He wrote in bursts, like someone catching his breath.
Right after Fire, he writes, in effect: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars. That's striking from a man who was a philosopher and a scholar.
He isn't throwing away his mind. He's saying what met him that night wasn't an idea he'd reasoned his way to. It was the God of a family story, who calls people by name.
Those three names come straight from scripture.

teach.h: THE BUSH THAT DIDN'T BURN UP.
teach.b: In Exodus, Moses sees a bush on fire that doesn't burn up. In the King James words, "the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed."

And the voice from the fire says, "I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Pascal's night echoes that scene: a fire, and a God known by the people he has met.
Further down, Pascal reaches for more words: certainty, feeling, joy, peace. Joy, again and again, and tears of joy.
Then he sews it into his coat, not to show anyone, but to keep it close. Some readers see the note as the hidden center of everything he wrote afterward. Nobody can say exactly what he saw.
He gave us one word for it, and kept it against his chest.

how: Pascal's note, often called the Memorial, is read by Christians of different churches as a witness to a personal encounter with God, and some keep a copy of it or a short line from scripture close by in a similar way.

games.q: you're a mathematician. something happened to you one night that you can't explain. what do you do with it?
o: write it down in a few words and keep it close.
games.why: Pascal wrote a short, broken note headed Fire, sewed it into his coat, and, the story goes, never mentioned it to anyone.

practice: Think of a moment you've never quite been able to explain: a moment of awe, of love, of being met, of clarity.

Don't tell yourself the whole story; let it come back in the quiet, and wait for one word to rise for it, the way Pascal had Fire. If you pray, hold that moment before God; if you don't, simply hold it and let the word arrive.

wordCard.voice: Pascal. The mathematician who had a night of fire, writing one word for what he felt and keeping it sewn into his coat.

carryVoice: Your line: fire. One word for a whole night, kept close. Day eight hundred ninety, done.
